title: North and South: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: Industrial Manchester and the Hale Family's Arrival

utterances.text: Welcome to North and South Unpacked — a close, passionate, and sometimes combative reading of Elizabeth Gaskell's great industrial novel.
I'm your host, and over this series we'll be following Margaret Hale — a rector's daughter from the rural south — as she's transplanted into the smoke and struggle of industrial Milton-Northern.
It's a novel about class, faith, pride, and the slow, sometimes excruciating education of two people who can barely stand each other.
Today we begin at the beginning — Margaret's world before the upheaval, and the first tremors of everything that's about to change.
I'm joined by three brilliant readers, each of whom brings something this novel demands.

Oliver Trevelyan has voiced more classic novels than almost anyone alive — he hears Gaskell's prose the way a musician hears a score, and his instinct for what's funny and what's genuinely moving is simply irreplaceable.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as maps of power — who holds it, who's crushed by it, and what the fiction is quietly admitting about both.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has re-read North and South more times than she'll admit — she brings a reader's love and a critic's precision in equal measure.
Let's begin where Gaskell begins — with Margaret, and with memory.
What strikes me first, every time, is how Gaskell introduces Margaret not in the present but through the past — through memory layered on memory.
We meet her in a nursery — already a room about childhood, about origins — and she's immediately transported nine years back.
Gaskell gives us this marvellous phrase — she was brought, she writes,
"all untamed from the forest."
Untamed from the forest — to share the polished world of Harley Street.
There's something almost fairy-tale in that — the wild child brought into civilization — and Gaskell plays it with enormous tenderness.
And then comes this passage about the nursery itself, which I think is one of the finest pieces of comic-gothic in the novel.
"She remembered the dark, dim look of the London nursery, presided over by an austere and ceremonious nurse, who was terribly particular about clean hands and torn frocks."
That nurse is the whole world of Harley Street compressed into one figure — correct, cold, obsessed with surfaces.
She appears for exactly one sentence and she tells you everything.
What Oliver says about surfaces is exactly right — and what moves me is what's underneath them.
That little girl of nine, crying bitterly but more quietly so as not to wake Edith — that detail of the suppressed grief is heartbreaking.
And then she hushes her sobs when her father comes in — not to distress him.
At nine years old, Margaret is already protecting the people she loves from her own pain.
That is Margaret's whole character, right there, in embryo.
And it prepares us for a passage that comes later in these opening chapters — where the suppression becomes almost cosmic.
When Margaret looks out at the night sky after her father's devastating announcement, Gaskell writes something extraordinary.

"Those never-ending depths of space, in their still serenity, were more mocking to her than any material bounds could be — shutting in the cries of earth's sufferers, which now might ascend into that infinite splendour of vastness and be lost — lost for ever, before they reached His throne."
That repetition — lost, lost for ever — is grief that has no container.
It's the same grief as the nine-year-old's, but now it fills the universe.
Both of those passages are telling us something specific about displacement — and it's not only psychological.
Margaret is uprooted at nine to serve the social requirements of a family above her in the hierarchy — the grander circumstances, Gaskell calls them, with pointed irony.
Her wardrobe must be arranged to suit those circumstances before her father can even visit.
The child's feelings are simply not part of the calculation.
That pattern — individual suffering subordinated to social obligation — runs through the entire novel.
What interests me about Caroline's passage is that when Margaret looks up at the void and finds no God, what she's actually confronting is the absence of any authority that cares.
The cries of earth's sufferers — Gaskell's phrase is precise — might be lost before they reach anyone who can hear them.
That's not a personal spiritual crisis — that's a crisis of legitimacy.
And it's exactly the crisis the factory workers of Milton-Northern are living through every day of the novel.
Daniel is right that Gaskell is drawing a map — but what I love is how she also draws a counterpoint.
Because while Margaret is staring into a void, Edith is in Corfu — and Gaskell gives us Edith's letter with barely suppressed comic delight.
Their most arduous duties, we're told, are boating, land-picnics, and copying out popular tunes for the bandmaster.
Gaskell writes it with a completely straight face — which is exactly what makes it so funny.
And then she gives us this image for Edith's life that is genuinely beautiful and also just slightly ruthless.
"Edith's life seemed like the deep vault of blue sky above her, free — utterly free from fleck or cloud."
Free — utterly free.
It's placed right next to Margaret's universe full of unanswered cries — the contrast couldn't be sharper or more pointed.
And it tells us something about what the novel thinks of ease.
Edith is not a villain — she's genuinely fond of Margaret, she's warm, she's happy.
But her happiness is effortless in a way the novel ultimately can't quite respect.
Gaskell is constructing a moral universe in which difficulty, doubt, and grief are the things that make you real.
And that is a very northern idea — even before Margaret has set foot anywhere near Milton.
There's one more passage that belongs in this conversation — and it's almost a comic coda to everything we've said.
Thornton, having met Margaret for the first time, walks away muttering to himself.
Gaskell gives us his interior monologue in a single devastating sentence.
"A more proud, disagreeable girl I never saw. Even her great beauty is blotted out of one's memory by her scornful ways."
He mentions her great beauty in the very sentence where he claims he's forgotten it.
The man is not as composed as he thinks he is.
And that gap — between what he says and what he reveals — is where the whole novel lives.
Pride, displacement, the void, and a man who protests too much — we are very much in Gaskell's hands already.
In our next segment, we'll move deeper into Milton itself — the smoke, the strikes, and the human cost of the industrial north.
Stay with us.

segments.title: The Mill Owner's Burden: Thornton and the Strike

utterances.text: Welcome back to North and South Unpacked.
We're exploring Elizabeth Gaskell's great industrial novel — the book that dares to put a cotton master and a clergyman's daughter in the same moral arena and watch the sparks fly.
With me today are three voices who know this novel deeply and bring very different things to it.
Oliver Trevelyan is an actor and writer who has voiced more classic novel audiobooks than anyone alive — he hears Gaskell's prose the way a musician hears a score.
Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class power — and North and South, he'll tell you, is one of the most searching of the lot.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read this novel as a teenager and has never quite let it go.
Today's segment: John Thornton — mill owner, self-made man, and one of Victorian fiction's most contested heroes.
We're looking at Thornton in conflict — with his workers, with Margaret, and with himself.
Daniel, let's start with you — because you've always argued that Thornton is more complicated than either his admirers or his critics allow.
Thank you — yes, and I think the complication starts very early in the novel, before the strike, before the riot.
There's a passage in Chapter Eleven where Margaret reports back to her father after that first dinner at the Thorntons'.
She's been repelled by Thornton's boasting about Milton, by his contempt for the improvident poor.
But then she catches herself — because one moment broke through the hardness.
She says — and Gaskell gives her extraordinary precision here —

"Everything else revolted me, from its hardness; but he spoke about himself so simply — with so little of the pretence that makes the vulgarity of shop-people, and with such tender respect for his mother."
That is a scalpel of a sentence.
Gaskell knows that what makes Thornton legible as a human being is not his achievements but his origins — the shop-boy who didn't forget where he came from.
And yet Margaret's critique is also devastating: he despises improvidence without once thinking it his duty to address it.
That is the precise charge that the whole novel will spend its remaining chapters trying to answer.
And what I love about that passage — as a performer — is the rhythm of Margaret's speech.
She builds her objections in a great rolling clause — Milton-boasting, contempt for the poor — and then she cuts herself off with that simple declaration.
"No! his statement of having been a shop-boy was the thing I liked best of all."
That "No!" at the start — it's a full stop and a reversal at once.
Gaskell writes dialogue the way good dramatists do — every punctuation mark is a stage direction.
And the comedy of it — Margaret is defending a man she finds insufferable, without quite realising she's doing it.
What moves me about this early passage is that it's the first crack in Margaret's armour.
She came into that dinner room fully prepared to dislike John Thornton.
And one unguarded moment of simplicity — the memory of his mother — undoes some of that.
But Daniel is right that the critique stands.
Thornton owes his position to his mother's training — Margaret says that plainly — and yet he extends no such training to those beneath him.
The novel is, in part, the story of Thornton learning that debt.
And speaking of his mother — there's that extraordinary passage in Chapter Twelve about Mrs. Thornton's relationship with her two children.
Gaskell dissects the way Mrs. Thornton loves — or rather, the way she cannot quite love — her daughter Fanny.
She has unconscious contempt for weakness, the narrator tells us — and Fanny is weak in precisely those points where mother and son are strong.
And yet the tenderness she reserves for Fanny — the "love" and "dear" — is really a form of shame.
The real pride, the real love, is in the line Gaskell gives the narrator — quietly, as if almost reluctant to say it aloud.
"Her heart gave thanks for him day and night; and she walked proudly among women for his sake."
No "love," no "dear" — just that biblical cadence.
This is where Gaskell shows us that the Thornton household is built on a kind of productive hardness — and that hardness has social consequences far beyond the family parlour.
That sentence is one of the great sentences in the novel, and I'll fight anyone who disagrees.
"She walked proudly among women for his sake" — it has the weight of a psalm.
Gaskell understands that the deepest pride is silent — it doesn't announce itself.
And it tells us something crucial about John: he was formed by someone who believed that character is demonstrated, not declared.
Which makes the riot scene all the more resonant — because that's where he has to act, not speak.
Let's go to that riot scene — Chapter Twenty-Two — because it's the moment everything boils over.
The striking workers are outside Marlborough Mills, the Irish hands have been brought in, and the crowd turns violent.
Daniel — the imagery Gaskell uses to describe what stops the mob is extraordinary.
It is extraordinary — and also, to my mind, deeply ambivalent.
What dissolves the mob's fury isn't the approach of soldiers — though that's mentioned — and it certainly isn't any act of Thornton's.
It is the sight of Margaret, wounded, her face upturned.
And Gaskell renders it with this almost unbearable slowness:

"that pale, upturned face, with closed eyes, still and sad as marble, though the tears welled out of the long entanglement of eyelashes, and dropped down; and, heavier, slower plash than even tears, came the drip of blood from her wound."
"Heavier, slower plash than even tears" — that's gothic writing of the highest order.
But notice who it serves: the master stands resolute, unmoved — and it is the female body that absorbs the violence and disperses it.
Even Boucher — the most desperate of them — is shamed into retreat not by argument or justice, but by spectacle.
Gaskell is a radical novelist, but she's not a simple one — and this scene shows the tension between her radicalism and her culture's instincts.
I hear what Daniel's saying, and I think he's right about the ambivalence.
But as a reader — as someone who has read that passage many times — what strikes me first is the sheer physical precision of it.
Gaskell slows time down to the drip of blood.
And the marble simile — still and sad as marble — it's not just decorative.
Marble is what you carve monuments from.
In this moment, Margaret is being turned into an image — which is exactly what Daniel is worried about, but it's also how great literature works on us.
It makes us feel something before we can argue about it.
And Thornton's response — the moment the retreat becomes a flight — is one line: "he darted up the steps to Margaret."
After all that slow horror, three words of motion.
Gaskell knows how to end a scene.
The restraint is everything — a lesser novelist gives us the embrace, the declaration.
Gaskell gives us a dart up three steps, and leaves the rest to us.
Now — the striker Nicholas Higgins has been circling this discussion.
He's the novel's great working-class voice, and Gaskell gives him his own kind of creed.
Daniel, before we get to the famous Chapter Fifty-One, can you tell us something about how Higgins is positioned in the novel?
Higgins is one of the most honestly drawn working-class characters in Victorian fiction — which is not faint praise.
He is materialist, unsentimentally so.
When Margaret meets him, he delivers what I can only call his philosophical manifesto:
"I believe what I see, and no more. That's what I believe, young woman. I don't believe all I hear — no! not by a big deal."
It sounds blunt — and it is — but read the rest of that passage.
He watched his sick daughter Bessy flush at the sound of a strange step — because she hoped it was Margaret coming to visit.
He noticed it. He kept it to himself. He waited to see if the promise would be kept.
That is not a man without tenderness — it is a man who has learned to keep his tenderness separate from his beliefs, because his life has taught him that false hope costs too much.
And the way he ends that speech — "hoo's welcome, as long as hoo'll keep from preaching on what hoo knows nought about" — it's magnificent.
He's welcoming and warning simultaneously.
And there's a kind of dignity in that directness — something Gaskell herself seems to admire, even as she gives Margaret the better arguments elsewhere.
Higgins and Thornton are mirror images, in a way.
Both hard men who conceal something softer.
Which is why their eventual reconciliation — in Chapter Thirty-Nine — feels so entirely earned.
Chapter Thirty-Nine is the passage I return to most often when people ask me if Gaskell is a radical novelist.
Thornton goes to find Higgins — to offer him work — but the narrator takes us inside his mind first.
He gave up two hours of his own labour to investigating Higgins's story — checking the facts, asking around.
That is a man who takes justice seriously as a practice, not just a sentiment.
But then Gaskell gives us this extraordinary admission about his interior life:

"He had tenderness in his heart — 'a soft place,' as Nicholas Higgins called it; but he had some pride in concealing it; he kept it very sacred and safe, and was jealous of every circumstance that tried to gain admission."
Sacred and safe.
These are words from the lexicon of private religion — and Gaskell applies them to a man's capacity for feeling.
That is not the psychology of a simple capitalist villain.
It is the psychology of someone who has armoured himself against disappointment — and is now, slowly, beginning to disarm.
And the irony that runs through that whole scene — Thornton is desperate for Margaret not to know that she's what brought him there.
He has convinced himself he's coming purely in the name of justice.
And then he walks through the door and there she is.
The comedy and the tragedy of it — they happen in the same beat.
And she passes out without a word, bowing her head to hide her pallor — and he bows equally low in return.
Two people keeping secrets from each other in a doorway.
It's almost Chekhovian.
And then, twenty chapters or so later, Thornton arrives at something that sounds almost like a programme for social reform.
Chapter Fifty-One — his speech to Margaret about institutions and personal contact.
Daniel, this is the passage you argue is the novel's thesis statement — or its closest approximation.
Its closest approximation — and its most honest limitation.
What Thornton says is remarkable.
He has come to believe that no institution, however well designed, can do what personal contact can do.
Here is the passage — and it deserves to be heard in full:

"I have arrived at the conviction that no mere institutions, however wise, and however much thought may have been required to organise and arrange them, can attach class to class as they should be attached, unless the working out of such institutions bring the individuals of the different classes into actual personal contact."
"Such intercourse is the very breath of life."
Now — that is a genuine intellectual development in this character.
He is not a man who began with this insight.
He had to be formed by events — by the strike, by Higgins, by watching Boucher's family — to arrive here.
My caveat is this: the solution he offers is still personal and paternalistic.
It is the master who brings the idea; the workers who participate in working it out.
There is no structural redistribution of power here — only a more humane exercise of the power that already exists.
And yet — and yet — read the end of that passage.
Thornton says something almost bashful at the close:
"We should understand each other better, and I'll venture to say we should like each other more."
"I'll venture to say" — that small hedge, from a man who almost never hedges.
It tells you how much this matters to him personally.
Daniel is right that it falls short of structural change.
But Gaskell is writing about what she believed was humanly possible — not what was politically ideal.
And in a novel, that distinction is where the drama lives.
What strikes me about this speech — and I've read it aloud several times — is how exhausted it sounds.
Not rhetorically exhausted — I mean a man who has worked through something.
The cadence is slower than Thornton's usual manner — he keeps qualifying, adding clauses.
It's the prose of a man who has stopped performing certainty.
And that — more than any argument about institutions — is what Gaskell has been building toward.
The man who could not see his duty to the poor he came from is now standing in a room, uncertain, reaching.
Uncertain, and reaching — that seems to me exactly the right note to leave Thornton on for this part of our conversation.
A self-made man in the process of remaking himself — which may be the most Victorian story of all, and the one Gaskell tells with the least sentimentality.
After the break, we'll be turning to Margaret Hale herself — the southern interloper who unsettles everyone she meets, and who is unsettled in return.
Stay with us.

segments.title: Class and Conscience: Higgins's Fight for Working Dignity

utterances.text: Welcome back to North and South Unpacked.
We've been tracing the great fault lines of Gaskell's novel — class, conscience, and the distance between South and North.
And now we arrive at one of the novel's most quietly radical moves: the friendship between Margaret Hale and the Higgins family.
A relationship built not on philanthropy or condescension, but on something rarer — genuine human recognition.
Oliver, I want to start with you, because the first meeting of Margaret and Higgins is pure performance on Gaskell's part.
What does she do in that opening encounter that no lesser novelist would have managed?
What she does is breathtakingly simple, and therefore almost impossible to imitate.
She doesn't contrive a dramatic meeting. She gives us a street, a crowd of mill workers, a series of unremarkable compliments.
And then, from within that noise, one voice emerges — a careworn man, addressing a girl who is smiling at some private thought.
Listen to how Gaskell phrases it — it's written for the voice, I promise you.
"You may well smile, my lass; many a one would smile to have such a bonny face."
There's a whole life in that sentence — exhaustion, gentleness, a man who has clearly lost more than he expects to recover.
And Gaskell doesn't over-explain it. She simply says he looked so careworn that Margaret could not help giving him an answering smile.
That's the whole of the first meeting. A shared smile across a social chasm. Magnificent economy.
And what strikes me every time I re-read those pages is what Gaskell pointedly does not give us.
They never exchange a word — she says that explicitly.
"They had never exchanged a word; nothing had been said but that first compliment."
Yet Margaret looks upon this man with more interest than upon anyone else in Milton.
More than Thornton. More than her neighbours. A man she doesn't even know by name yet.
That's Gaskell quietly insisting on the priority of common humanity over social category.
And then the flowers. That scene with Bessy is so tender it almost hurts.
Margaret has gathered these hedge and ditch flowers — dog-violets, celandines — with what Gaskell calls an unspoken lament for the sweet profusion of the South.
And she simply gives them away. On impulse. To a girl she barely knows.
The pale blue eyes lightened up — that phrase. I re-read it every time.
I want to be careful here, though, because what Gaskell is doing is more complicated than simple benevolence.
Margaret brings South into North, quite literally — she arrives carrying flowers from the fields, the natural world that Milton has largely paved over.
And Bessy, the ailing daughter — already a figure produced by the cotton fluff in the mills — receives those flowers like a form of oxygen.
Now, one reading of this is purely sentimental: the kind lady from the South soothes the suffering poor.
But Gaskell's language resists that. Margaret is described as acting on a sudden impulse — not charity, not design. Impulse.
The transaction isn't top-down. The connection that follows is reciprocal, and that changes everything politically.
And what confirms that reciprocity — what seals it — is where Gaskell takes us afterwards.
Margaret walks home, and Gaskell gives us this extraordinary passage about what Milton has now become to her.
"From that day Milton became a brighter place to her. It was not the long, bleak sunny days of spring, nor yet was it that time was reconciling her to the town of her habitation."
"It was that in it she had found a human interest."
A human interest. Not a worthy cause. Not a lesson. A human interest.
Gaskell is doing something almost Wordsworthian there — meaning grows from encounter, not from argument.
Wordsworthian is exactly right. And I love that Gaskell explicitly rules out the alternatives.
It wasn't the arrival of spring. It wasn't the simple passage of time softening things.
She names what it actually was. That grammatical precision — it was that — feels like a quiet insistence.
Gaskell will not let us mistake sentiment for the real thing. She insists you locate the exact source.
And then we jump forward to the final chapters — Thornton's failure, his reckoning — and Gaskell brings all of this to a point.
Thornton, stripped of his mill, his position, his mastery — speaks with a clarity he couldn't have managed before.
He tells Colthurst what he actually wants now, and it's not profit, not power — it's something almost embarrassingly modest.
"My only wish is to have the opportunity of cultivating some intercourse with the hands beyond the mere 'cash nexus.'"
Cash nexus — Gaskell borrows Carlyle's phrase and puts it in Thornton's mouth as something to be transcended.
The manufacturers around him shake their heads at this as though it were dangerous radicalism.
And Gaskell is absolutely clear-eyed about that irony: the mildest humanism reads as a threat to the system.
And then there's the round-robin. I find that detail almost unbearably moving.
Thornton tells Margaret about it — and his pleasure in telling her is part of the beauty of the moment.
He says — and notice the little parenthesis Gaskell drops in, almost conspiratorial:
"I had a round-robin from some of my men — I suspect in Higgins' handwriting — stating their wish to work for me, if ever I was in a position to employ men again on my own behalf."
"That was good, wasn't it?"
That was good, wasn't it. Three words that carry the entire weight of everything Thornton has learned.
He needs her to confirm it. The man who commanded hundreds now asks a woman if his workers' loyalty was worth something.
And I suspect in Higgins' handwriting — that suspicion is so tender.
Higgins, the union man, the strike organiser, the voice of collective labour — writing out his men's loyalty to their master in his own hand.
It doesn't cancel out the conflict that came before. It doesn't resolve it cheaply.
It says: the relationship between these men has grown into something that outlasts the structures that defined it.
Which is exactly what happened between Margaret and Higgins, from that very first smile on a Milton street.
I'd only add: Gaskell is honest about the limits too.
The system itself isn't transformed. Thornton's experiments are still just that — experiments — held at arm's length by the other manufacturers.
He describes them as what Archimedes sought — the fixed point from which to move the earth.
That's a staggering image to use for a conversation between master and worker over a canteen dinner.
But I think Gaskell means it. She is saying: if you could change the human texture of these relations, you change everything.
Whether that's utopian or radical depends on what you believe is possible. And she leaves that question open.
Utopian or radical — and perhaps both at once.
That question of what transformation looks like — personal, structural, or some fragile combination — will carry us into our next section.
We'll be looking at how Gaskell handles the language of power itself — and what it costs her characters to speak across the divide.

segments.title: Margaret's Pivot: Authority, Duty, and Self-Discovery

utterances.text: Welcome to North and South Unpacked — the programme where we take Elizabeth Gaskell's great industrial novel apart, passage by passage, to see how it works.
I'm your host, and today we're examining what might be called Margaret Hale's pivot — the chapters where we watch a young woman discover the full dimensions of her own character.
Joining me today are three exceptional readers of this novel.
Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the voice of more classic novel audiobooks than anyone alive — who hears Gaskell's prose the way most of us hear music.
Dr. Daniel Rosen — cultural historian — who reads every drawing-room scene as a map of class power and every act of charity as a political act.
And Caroline Woodcourt — book critic and lifelong re-reader of this novel — who cares above all about what a sentence does to you when you encounter it on the page.
We begin in Chapter Ten — a tea table, a bracelet, and the first real collision between Margaret Hale and John Thornton.
Chapter Ten is one of the great comic-tender scenes in Victorian fiction, and I don't think it gets nearly enough credit.
You have this enormous, serious-minded mill owner — Thornton — and he is utterly undone by a bracelet sliding down a woman's wrist.
Gaskell writes that he watched it with — listen to this — she says:
"It seemed as if it fascinated him to see her push it up impatiently until it tightened her soft flesh; and then to mark the loosening—the fall."
The loosening — the fall. Gaskell could have written a whole sentence there. She gave us three words.
And then she gives Thornton that tiny internal exclamation: "There it goes again!" — which is the funniest moment of repressed longing in the whole novel.
What strikes me every time I re-read that scene is the doubling of it — his fascination set against her complete indifference to him.
She's managing a headache, she's managing the tea, she's managing her anxiety about her father's new friendship.
And then Gaskell gives us this extraordinary image of social performance — "She handed him his cup of tea with the proud air of an unwilling slave."
An unwilling slave. That phrase does so much work. It's comic and it's slightly devastating at the same time.
She's fulfilling her duty — she's genuinely attending to whether his cup is empty — but her whole soul is in revolt against the obligation.
I want to press on that phrase — unwilling slave — because Gaskell doesn't use it casually.
In a novel that is fundamentally about the conditions of labour — about who serves and who commands — to describe a gentlewoman at a tea table in those terms is a provocation.
Margaret's subjection is framed as gentility — as a performance of class refinement — but the word "slave" names what it actually is.
The drawing room and the factory floor are not as far apart as either Margaret or Thornton yet understands.
That tension between duty as performance and duty as something deeper and more costly runs right through these chapters.
And we see it extend into the domestic space in Chapter Eleven, when Margaret begins to understand what her mother is concealing.
Chapter Eleven is where the novel first becomes genuinely frightening for me.
There's that terrible moment when Margaret follows Dixon out of her mother's room and pushes open the door and finds her mother on her knees.
And Gaskell — very quietly — tells us:
"she caught a few words which were evidently a prayer for strength and patience to endure severe bodily suffering."
She doesn't give us the prayer. She gives us Margaret overhearing it. That restraint is devastating.
And then Margaret lies awake all night making practical plans — a new servant, better domestic arrangements — because that is how she processes grief. She organises.
The thing about reading that scene aloud — and I have — is that the prose is almost unbearably careful around the word suffering.
Gaskell has been building up the texture of Milton life — the bad air, the sordid domestic worries, the wrench from Helstone — and then she lands on "severe bodily suffering" like a door closing.
And it is exactly that quality — the door closing — that signals to the audience this is no longer a novel of manners. Death has entered.
Margaret doesn't know yet how serious it is. But we do. That dramatic irony is exquisitely handled.
I think we should also notice what Gaskell says about the cause of Mrs. Hale's decline — because she is precise about it.
It's not simply illness in the abstract. It is Milton. It is the air of a manufacturing town, the "sordid form" of domestic worry in a place built for profit, not for human habitation.
Gaskell is arguing — quietly but unmistakably — that industrialisation has costs that are paid in bodies.
Mrs. Hale is a gentlewoman displaced by her husband's crisis of faith. But her suffering rhymes with the suffering of the mill workers. It is the same economy exacting its toll.
That word suffering carries us directly into the chapter where Margaret first refuses to be silent about what she sees — the confrontation with Thornton over the North and the South.
Caroline, you wanted to read from that passage.
I did — because it's one of the few moments in the early novel where Margaret's voice is completely unguarded.
Gaskell tells us she's been roused to — and I love this phrase — "a fond vehemence of defence" that brings angry tears into her eyes.
And then she says this:
"I see men here going about in the streets who look ground down by some pinching sorrow or care—who are not only sufferers but haters."
"Now, in the South we have our poor, but there is not that terrible expression in their countenances of a sullen sense of injustice which I see here."
Sufferers but haters. That conjunction is astonishing. She's not pitying these men — she's diagnosing them.
And then she collapses into — Gaskell's own phrase — "a determined silence" and is angry with herself for having said so much.
It's a perfect dramatic rhythm. The eruption, the argument, the retreat. And the retreat is almost funnier than the eruption.
She's just delivered what is essentially a political speech at a tea table. And now she's mortified.
But Thornton has heard her. And that changes everything.
What I want to insist on is that Margaret is not wrong in what she observes — and Gaskell is not simply sentimentalising the South.
She is describing a specific phenomenon — the expression on the faces of men who know they are being exploited and cannot articulate it in any language the powerful will recognise.
"A sullen sense of injustice" — that is not ignorance or ingratitude. That is class consciousness without a political vehicle.
And here's the thing: Margaret is a gentlewoman from the South, completely outside the system of production — and she sees it immediately.
Thornton — who runs the mill — has organised it out of his field of vision. That's the novel's central irony in these early chapters.
And the novel will test that vision of Margaret's in the most extreme way possible — in the riot scene of Chapter Twenty-Two.
Where she steps out onto a doorstep and puts her body between Thornton and the mob.
Chapter Twenty-Two is where the novel earns its right to everything that comes before it.
And Gaskell describes the moment Margaret is struck with a sentence of almost biblical economy:
"A sharp pebble flew by her, grazing forehead and cheek, and drawing a blinding sheet of light before her eyes."
A blinding sheet of light. Not darkness. Light.
There's something almost visionary in that image — she doesn't collapse into darkness, she's annihilated by brightness.
And then what Thornton does in that scene — the way Gaskell renders his interior — is one of the most startling passages in Victorian fiction.
He carries her in and lays her down — and Gaskell says he is "looking on her pure white face" when it comes upon him.
And then — not in a letter, not in a proposal — he simply speaks it aloud in an empty room:
"Oh, my Margaret—my Margaret! no one can tell what you are to me! Dead—cold as you lie there, you are the only woman I ever loved!"
He says it to an unconscious woman. It's as raw as anything in the novel. He can't help himself.
What I find striking about that moment is the detail Gaskell gives us just before it — his anger hasn't abated.
He's thinking about the troops arriving five minutes too late. He's still calculating authority and order.
And then — "the sense of what she was to him came upon him so keenly that he spoke it out in his pain."
Pain. Not tenderness, not joy — pain. Because loving Margaret, for Thornton, is a form of suffering he cannot master.
The mill owner who controls everything cannot control this. And that is where the novel begins to crack him open.
The woman who handed him tea with the proud air of an unwilling slave has, by Chapter Twenty-Two, shed blood for him.
And neither of them can quite account for what that means — not yet.
That's where we'll leave Margaret for now — between the drawing room and the doorstep, between duty performed and duty chosen.
We'll be back shortly to explore what the novel makes of the North itself — its labour, its pride, and its cost.

segments.title: Wit, Irony, and the Dangers of Misunderstanding

utterances.text: Welcome back to North and South Unpacked.
We've been tracing the great fault lines of Gaskell's novel — class, industry, suffering.
But North and South is also, quietly, one of the funniest novels of the Victorian era.
And this segment belongs to Oliver Trevelyan — actor, audiobook narrator, and the person in this room most likely to catch what Gaskell wrote for the voice rather than the page.
Oliver, you've been sitting on your hands for the last twenty minutes.
What's the first thing you want us to hear?
The first thing I want you to hear is Mrs. Thornton, alone in a room she's just been swept out of — by a girl who doesn't even own the room.
That is a comic situation of the first order.
Gaskell sets it up beautifully: Margaret exits, and I quote —
"She swept out of it with the noiseless grace of an offended princess."
Offended princess — in someone else's house — leaving the grande dame standing there with absolutely nowhere to go.
Gaskell gives us the punchline without cracking a smile: "There was nothing for it but to show herself out."
Seven words of perfect social humiliation, delivered as plain narration.
And what I love is that Mrs. Thornton is secretly delighted.
She has, as Gaskell says, "quite enough of natural humour" to appreciate being bested.
And what follows in her interior monologue is extraordinary.
She thinks to herself — and I want to read this because the rhythm of it matters —
"My young lady, you've a pretty good temper of your own. If John and you had come together, he would have had to keep a tight hand over you, to make you know your place."
This is a woman who has just been defied — and she is practically purring.
She respects Margaret more in this moment of anger than she ever has in politeness.
And then she turns to Fanny — her own daughter — and the contrast is merciless.
I want to hold that image of Mrs. Thornton a moment longer — because it tells us something structurally important.
She respects Margaret not because of warmth or goodness, but because Margaret has mastered the performance of class dominance.
Pride and spirit, as Mrs. Thornton calls them, are the currencies of the powerful — and Margaret spends them fluently.
The comedy sits on top of something rather more unsettling.
Meanwhile, on the other side of the novel entirely, Nicholas Higgins is making an argument about justice in an entirely different register.
He says to Margaret — and I'm quoting him directly —

"I take up John Boucher's cause, as lives next door but one, wi' a sickly wife, and eight childer, none on 'em factory age; and I don't take up his cause only, though he's a poor good-for-nought — but I take up th' cause o' justice."
He knows every name, every sick child, every broken circumstance.
And the novel holds those two worlds — Mrs. Thornton's drawing-room theatre and Higgins's doorstep solidarity — inside the same covers.
When I read Higgins aloud, that speech is genuinely moving — but it's also written for performance.
Notice the self-deprecating sting: he calls Boucher "a poor good-for-nought, as can only manage two looms at a time."
He insults the man he's sacrificing for — and it somehow makes the love in it more real, not less.
Gaskell is too good a dramatic writer to give us uncomplicated nobility.
Higgins grumbles. He grimaces. He still strikes.
Can we talk about Thornton? Because the misunderstanding comedy in this novel reaches its peak with him.
There's a scene at a dinner — he shakes Margaret's hand for the first time.
And Gaskell tells us: he knew it was the first time their hands had met, though she was perfectly unconscious of the fact.
This enormous man — this captain of industry — is cataloguing the exact quality of a handshake she has already forgotten.
And then he composes himself, turns his back, and — I'll read this —

"he saw his sister's restless way of continually arranging some part of her gown, her wandering eyes, now glancing here, now there, but without any purpose in her observation; and he contrasted them uneasily with the large soft eyes that looked forth steadily at one object, as if from out their light beamed some gentle influence of repose."
He is supposedly not looking at Margaret. He is comprehensively looking at Margaret.
And then, beautifully, he sighs — and "threw himself, with an effort, but with all his heart and soul, into a conversation with Mr. Hale."
Poor Mr. Hale. He has no idea what kind of conversation he's receiving.
And on the other side of that coin — Margaret thinking she's invisible.
There's a later scene where she stands behind her father, barely moving, entirely convinced Thornton hasn't noticed her.
Gaskell lets the irony detonate in a single parenthetical aside:
"As if he did not feel the consciousness of her presence all over, though his eyes had never rested on her!"
The exclamation mark is doing extraordinary work there.
The narrator is barely containing herself.
It's the closest Gaskell comes to nudging the reader in the ribs — and it's entirely, precisely earned.
What strikes me — and I mean this seriously — is how the irony around Thornton and Margaret functions as a pressure release valve.
We laugh at Thornton's suppressed longing. We are charmed by it.
And that charm does real ideological work — it softens a man who, in the same chapters, is plotting to break a strike.
The novel knows this. I think Gaskell knew this.
She gives us Higgins's answer, and she gives us Thornton's longing — and she lets us feel the tension between them rather than resolving it cheaply.
And that tension — between the comic and the serious, the intimate and the structural — is perhaps what makes North and South so persistently readable.
We'll be picking up that thread when we come back — turning to the question of what Gaskell's irony costs her characters, and what it gives them.

segments.title: North Meets South: Reconciliation and the Cost of Progress

utterances.text: Welcome back to North and South Unpacked.
We've spent much of this series tracing the fault lines — class, region, labour, faith.
Today we turn to something harder to name: the moments when those fault lines begin, tentatively, painfully, to close.
Reconciliation — between classes, between strangers, between the self and the world one has judged too quickly.
With me today, as ever, are Oliver Trevelyan, whose ear for Gaskell's rhythms I trust above all others.
Daniel Rosen, who will not let us be comfortable about what progress actually costs.
And Caroline Woodcourt, who has lived with this novel long enough to catch what first-time readers almost always miss.
Let's begin with first impressions — and how radically Gaskell destabilises them.
What strikes me every time I return to these early chapters is how honestly Gaskell renders Margaret's pride.
She doesn't sentimentalise it. Margaret looks at Thornton and her instinct is to assess, to rank.
And yet — even in the act of ranking him — she finds herself revising.
There's this wonderful moment where she tells her mother what she sees in his face.
"With such an expression of resolution and power, no face, however plain in feature, could be either vulgar or common."
She's giving him something — acknowledging something real — while still, brilliantly, holding him at arm's length.
"I should not like to have to bargain with him."
That tiny confession says everything about where she still is — and where she is about to go.
And notice what she calls him — in the very same breath.
"Altogether a man who seems made for his niche, mamma — sagacious, and strong, as becomes a great tradesman."
A great tradesman. Said to his face, essentially. Said to his face through mamma, which is somehow worse.
There's a comedy in it — Gaskell is absolutely aware of the comedy — but it's perfectly precise social comedy.
Margaret is praising him into a box. A very well-crafted, very condescending box.
And of course the entire novel is the story of her having to climb out of that box herself.
I want to sit with "made for his niche" for a moment, because that phrase carries real ideological weight.
Margaret is reading Thornton through a framework that naturalises class position — he belongs there, in trade, by virtue of what he is.
It's a profoundly conservative thought dressed up as a compliment.
And Gaskell knows this — which is why she immediately begins dismantling it, from both ends of the class hierarchy.
Look at what Margaret says just one chapter later — defending herself against her mother's snobbery about domestic work.
"I am myself a born and bred lady through it all, even though it comes to scouring a floor, or washing dishes."
That's Margaret asserting that class is character — not occupation, not labour, not the thing you do with your hands.
It's more radical than it sounds. And it cuts both ways.
It does cut both ways — and Gaskell makes sure we feel the irony.
Because in the very same passage, Margaret says of Thornton — quite tenderly, actually — that he can't help being in trade.
"I don't suppose his education would fit him for much else."
She means it kindly. That's the devastating part.
The condescension is entirely unconscious — and Gaskell places it immediately after Margaret's most fiercely egalitarian declaration.
She is the most unreliable idealist in Victorian fiction. And I mean that as the highest possible praise.
Which brings us, beautifully, to the other great idealist in the novel — Mrs. Thornton.
Who is not unreliable at all. Mrs. Thornton is absolutely, ferociously reliable. She knows exactly what she thinks.
And Gaskell gives her this extraordinary private tirade that I could read aloud every day for the rest of my life.
She is raging about Margaret's attitude to her son, and she turns to herself — there's no one else there — and she declares:
"Boy and man, he's the noblest, stoutest heart I ever knew. I don't care if I am his mother; I can see what's what, and not be blind."
"I don't care if I am his mother." The pre-emptive self-defence! She knows she's biased. She doesn't care.
And then — just to make sure we've understood — she ends with three words: "I hate her."
No qualification. No apology. Perfect.
And yet what's remarkable is that Mrs. Thornton and Margaret are mirrors of each other — both defined by ferocious loyalty, both blinded by it.
The class war between them is also, at some level, a recognition scene — two people who are fundamentally the same, unable to see it.
What Gaskell refuses to do — and this is her radicalism — is resolve that tension cheaply.
Mrs. Thornton never fully forgives Margaret. And that refusal is honest.
Reconciliation in this novel is never complete — it is always partial, always costly.
Which is exactly where I want to bring in the passage I love most in this segment — Thornton telling Margaret about the dining room.
Because here is what reconciliation actually looks like in Gaskell — not a grand gesture, not a speech, not a moment of weeping.
It looks like a man swallowing his pride over a canteen.
It starts, as so much in this novel starts, with a specific physical detail that Gaskell cannot resist.
"I saw such a miserable black frizzle of a dinner — a greasy cinder of meat."
"A greasy cinder of meat." That is not the language of a mill-owner's report. That is the language of a man who looked, and who felt something.
And then Higgins — the enemy, the strike organiser — walks in and proposes the same scheme Thornton had already designed.
And Thornton — this inflexible man, this man Margaret said she would not want to bargain with — quietly steps aside.
He takes the part of a steward. To a club proposed by his own workers.
If that isn't the most quietly extraordinary act in the whole novel, I honestly don't know what is.
And he does it with such — I almost want to say grace, but that's not quite right for Thornton.
He admits he was "a little riled" — that magnificent understatement.
And then he says he thought of throwing the whole thing overboard — and chose not to.
Gaskell lets us hear him reasoning his way through the temptation in real time.
"It seemed childish to relinquish a plan which I had once thought wise and well-laid, just because I myself did not receive all the honour."
He calls his own pride childish. To Margaret. That is the measure of how far he has come.
I want to take that a step further — because what Thornton is describing is a structural concession, not just a personal one.
He moves from owner — originator — to steward. The plan becomes the workers' plan.
That's not nothing. In the language of nineteenth-century industrial relations, that is a genuinely radical relinquishment of authority.
And yet — and I keep coming back to this — it is still Thornton who buys the provisions wholesale.
The capital still flows through him. The power is softened, humanised — but not dissolved.
Gaskell sees further than most Victorian novelists. But the limits of her imagining are still the limits of her world.
That tension — between the transformative and the structural, between what's changed and what hasn't — feels like exactly the right place to pause.
We've watched Margaret revise her first impression, Thornton revise his idea of authority, and Mrs. Thornton — magnificently — refuse to revise anything at all.
Coming up: we'll look at what Gaskell makes of the South itself — and whether Milton-Northern's noise and squalor is merely a backdrop, or something far more morally charged.
We've spent this episode tracking the fault lines in North and South — of class, of pride, of region, of feeling.
But as we close, I want to sit with what Gaskell chose not to resolve — the tensions she left deliberately alive in the novel's final pages.
Oliver, you've been the voice of Gaskell's comedy today — let's begin with you.
What strikes me, coming back to the very early scenes with fresh eyes, is how much of the novel's unresolved tension is planted in the very first meeting between Margaret and Thornton.
And Gaskell has the wit to let Thornton himself describe it — to his mother, no less — with just a touch of wounded masculine bafflement.
He says, with a short scornful laugh, that she treated him with contempt.
"She treated me with a haughty civility which had a strong flavour of contempt in it. She held herself aloof from me as if she had been a queen, and I her humble, unwashed vassal."
Unwashed vassal — that is superb. Gaskell is laughing at both of them simultaneously.
Thornton's pride is wounded, and he knows it, and the comedy is that his wounded pride is itself a form of vanity.
The resolution at the end of the novel doesn't entirely dissolve that first contempt — it just transforms it into something far more interesting.
And what makes it so much richer is that Gaskell shows us Margaret noticing Thornton before she'll admit she's noticing him.
There's that extraordinary passage where she's watching him beside her father — comparing their faces, their lines, their eyes — with a kind of involuntary intensity.
Gaskell writes it as if Margaret is simply an objective observer.
"The straight brows fell low over the clear, deep-set, earnest eyes, which without being unpleasantly sharp, seemed intent enough to penetrate into the very heart and core of what he was looking at."
She's supposed to be describing a face. She is describing a face. And yet.
The whole passage vibrates with everything Margaret won't say about what she sees.
That's something Gaskell never fully resolves — this habit Margaret has of understanding everything except her own heart.
I want to come at this from a slightly different angle, because I think the most unresolved thing in the novel is not the love story at all.
It's the question of what the South actually is — and what it does to the people trapped in it.
There's a passage late in the novel where Margaret is trying to dissuade Higgins from emigrating south, and she speaks with a ferocity that I think surprises even her.

"Those that have lived there all their lives, are used to soaking in the stagnant waters. They labour on from day to day, in the great solitude of steaming fields — never speaking or lifting up their poor, bent, downcast heads."
Stagnant waters. Bent heads. This is not pastoral idyll — this is a vision of spiritual annihilation.
And the novel never quite reckons with the fact that the North's industrial vigour is built on the bodies of people who might otherwise have been those bent, downcast labourers.
Gaskell sees it. She almost says it. But the romance pulls the conclusion elsewhere.
Daniel's right that the romance pulls focus — but I'd argue that's part of Gaskell's genius, not her evasion.
She gives us Margaret's interiority so completely that we live inside the contradiction.
That passage after the riot — when Margaret is alone, interrogating herself about why she stepped into the crowd — is one of the most honest pieces of self-examination in Victorian fiction.
"I, who hate scenes — I, who have despised people for showing emotion — who have thought them wanting in self-control — I went down and must needs throw myself into the melée, like a romantic fool!"
A romantic fool — she calls herself a romantic fool! And the anguish is real.
But the comedy is also real — the comedy of a person whose self-image is the very last thing to catch up with her heart.
What gets me every time is the physical detail at the end of that passage.
Margaret covers her face with her hands — and when she takes them away, the palms are wet with scalding tears.
Scalding. Not weeping — scalding.
That word does everything. It tells us the shame is burning, physical, beyond her control.
And Gaskell never quite lets Margaret escape that tension — between the woman who despises emotion and the woman who feels everything.
The resolution in the final chapters softens it. It doesn't remove it.
And I think that's ultimately what makes North and South a great novel rather than merely a good one.
Gaskell doesn't tie things off. She shows us a world in the middle of its own transformation — industrial, social, personal — and she has the courage to leave the seams showing.
The workers are still hungry. The South is still stagnant. Margaret is still, at some level, bewildered by herself.
Love doesn't fix the machinery. It just makes it briefly, radiantly bearable.
Love doesn't fix the machinery — I think that may be the finest summary of this novel I've ever heard.
Oliver Trevelyan, Daniel Rosen, Caroline Woodcourt — thank you all.
You've brought to North and South exactly the kind of attention it deserves — rigorous, warm, and alive to its comedy as much as its weight.
Elizabeth Gaskell spent a career insisting that the people her society preferred not to see were worth the full force of a great novelist's scrutiny.
North and South remains her most searching argument for that conviction.
Thank you for listening to North and South Unpacked.

c1:p11.text:
Margaret went up into the old nursery at the very top of the house,
where Newton was busy getting up some laces which were required for the
wedding. While Newton went (not without a muttered grumbling) to undo
the shawls, which had already been exhibited four or five times that
day, Margaret looked round upon the nursery; the first room in that
house with which she had become familiar nine years ago, when she was
brought, all untamed from the forest, to share the home, the play, and
the lessons of her cousin Edith. She remembered the dark, dim look of
the London nursery, presided over by an austere and ceremonious nurse,
who was terribly particular about clean hands and torn frocks. She
recollected the first tea up there—separate from her father and aunt,
who were dining somewhere down below, an infinite depth of stairs; for
unless she were up in the sky (the child thought), they must be deep
down in the bowels of the earth. At home—before she came to live in
Harley Street—her mother’s dressing-room had been her nursery; and as
they kept early hours in the country parsonage, Margaret had always had
her meals with her father and mother. Oh! well did the tall stately girl
of eighteen remember the tears shed with such wild passion of grief by
the little girl of nine, as she hid her face under the bed-clothes in
that first night; and how she was bidden not to cry by the nurse,
because it would disturb Miss Edith; and how she had cried as bitterly,
but more quietly, till her newly-seen, grand, pretty aunt had come
softly upstairs with Mr. Hale to show him his little sleeping daughter.
Then the little Margaret had hushed her sobs, and tried to lie quiet as
if asleep, for fear of making her father unhappy by her grief, which she
dared not express before her aunt, and which she rather thought it was
wrong to feel at all after the long hoping, and planning, and contriving
they had gone through at home, before her wardrobe could be arranged to
suit her grander circumstances, and before papa could leave his parish
to come up to London, even for a few days.
c1:p11.summary: Margaret ascends to the nursery where Newton prepares shawls and reflects on her painful arrival in London nine years ago, separated from her parents and country home.
c1:p11.best_quote: She remembered the dark, dim look of the London nursery, presided over by an austere and ceremonious nurse, who was terribly particular about clean hands and torn frocks

c5:p8.text:
She looked out upon the dark-grey lines of the church towers, square and
straight in the centre of the view, cutting against the deep blue
transparent depths beyond, into which she gazed, and felt that she might
gaze for ever, seeing at every moment some farther distance, and yet no
sign of God! It seemed to her at the moment, as if the earth was more
utterly desolate than if girt in by an iron dome, behind which there
might be the ineffaceable peace and glory of the Almighty: those
never-ending depths of space, in their still serenity, were more mocking
to her than any material bounds could be—shutting in the cries of
earth’s sufferers, which now might ascend into that infinite splendour
of vastness and be lost—lost for ever, before they reached His throne.
In this mood her father came in unheard. The moonlight was strong enough
to let him see his daughter in her unusual place and attitude. He came
to her and touched her shoulder before she was aware that he was there.
c5:p8.summary: Margaret gazes at the night sky in despair, unable to discern God's presence; her father silently enters and asks her to pray with him.

c8:p12.text:
Edith wrote fluently and well, if not graphically. She could not only
seize the salient and characteristic points of a scene, but she could
enumerate enough of indiscriminate particular for Margaret to make it
out for herself. Captain Lennox and another lately married officer
shared a villa, high up on the beautiful precipitous rocks overhanging
the sea. Their days, late as it was in the year, seemed spent in boating
or land-picnics; all out-of-doors, pleasure-seeking and glad, Edith’s
life seemed like the deep vault of blue sky above her, free—utterly
free from fleck or cloud. Her husband had to attend drill, and she, the
most musical officer’s wife there, had to copy the new and popular tunes
out of the most recent English music, for the benefit of the bandmaster;
those seemed their most severe and arduous duties. She expressed an
affectionate hope that, if the regiment stopped another year at Corfu,
Margaret might come out and pay her a long visit. She asked Margaret if
she remembered the day twelve-month on which she, Edith, wrote—how it
rained all day long in Harley Street; and how she would not put on her
new gown to go to a stupid dinner, and get it all wet and splashed in
going to the carriage; and how at that very dinner they had first met
Captain Lennox.
c8:p12.summary: Edith's letter describes her idyllic life in Corfu with her new husband, pleasures, and music, contrasting sharply with Margaret's dreary present.
c8:p12.best_quote: Edith's life seemed like the deep vault of blue sky above her, free—utterly free from fleck or cloud

that account of himself better than anything else he said. Everything
else revolted me, from its hardness; but he spoke about himself so
simply—with so little of the pretence that makes the vulgarity of
shop-people, and with such tender respect for his mother, that I was
less likely to leave the room then than when he was boasting about
Milton, as if there was not such another place in the world; or quietly
professing to despise people for careless, wasteful improvidence,
without ever seeming to think it his duty to try to make them
different,—to give them anything of the training which his mother gave
him, and to which he evidently owes his position, whatever that may be.
No! his statement of having been a shop-boy was the thing I liked best
of all.”

c12:p10.text:
Mrs. Thornton was silent after this; for her last words bore relation to
a subject which mortified her. She had an unconscious contempt for a
weak character; and Fanny was weak in the very points in which her
mother and brother were strong. Mrs. Thornton was not a woman much
given to reasoning; her quick judgment and firm resolution served her in
good stead of any long arguments and discussions with herself; she felt
instinctively that nothing could strengthen Fanny to endure hardships
patiently, or face difficulties bravely; and though she winced as she
made this acknowledgment to herself about her daughter, it only gave her
a kind of pitying tenderness of manner towards her; much of the same
description of demeanour with which mothers are wont to treat their weak
and sickly children. A stranger, a careless observer might have
considered that Mrs. Thornton’s manner to her children betokened far
more love to Fanny than to John. But such a one would have been deeply
mistaken. The very daringness with which mother and son spoke out
unpalatable truths, the one to the other, showed a reliance on the firm
centre of each other’s souls, which the uneasy tenderness of Mrs.
Thornton’s manner to her daughter, the shame with which she thought to
hide the poverty of her child in all the grand qualities which she
herself possessed unconsciously, and which she set so high a value upon
in others—this shame, I say, betrayed the want of a secure
resting-place for her affection. She never called her son by any name
but John; “love,” and “dear,” and such like terms, were reserved for
Fanny. But her heart gave thanks for him day and night; and she walked
proudly among women for his sake.
c12:p10.summary: The narrator analyzes Mrs. Thornton's conflicted feelings toward her daughter's weakness and her deep, undemonstrative pride in her son's strength; her affection for Fanny betrays insecurity about her daughter's lack of merit.

But the retrograde movement towards the gate had begun—as
unreasoningly, perhaps as blindly, as the simultaneous anger. Or,
perhaps, the idea of the approach of the soldiers, and the sight of that
pale, upturned face, with closed eyes, still and sad as marble, though
the tears welled out of the long entanglement of eyelashes, and dropped
down; and, heavier, slower plash than even tears, came the drip of blood
from her wound. Even the most desperate—Boucher himself—drew back,
faltered away, scowled, and finally went off, muttering curses on the
master, who stood in his unchanging attitude, looking after their
retreat with defiant eyes. The moment that retreat had changed into a
